newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota units' profits jump, better profits seen.
newsitem.headline: Toyota units' profits jump, better profits seen.

text.p: Most Toyota Motor Corp affiliates enjoyed big profit increases in 1996/97, helped by higher vehicle output at the parent firm and a weak yen, and see better profits ahead, the companies said on Wednesday.

Denso Corp, a major maker of electronic car components such as air conditioners, said it boosted its parent current profit to 100.35 billion yen ($843 million) in the year to March 31, up 44 percent from the previous year.

"Higher profits and sales in 1996/97 were due to increased component sales not only to Toyota but to other Japanese carmakers such as Honda, and to the weak yen," said a spokesman for Denso. Toyota owns 23 percent of Denso and Robert Bosch owns 5.4 percent, the spokesman said.

Denso forecast profits of 102 billion yen ($857 million) for 1997/98, up 1.6 percent. "We expect almost flat profits and sales for this year because of the anticipated impact of the sales tax rise on domestic car sales," the spokesman said. Denso supplies components to all Japanese carmakers except Nissan. Toyota accounts for 50 percent of its sales.
Car industry analysts expect Japan's vehicle output in 1997/98 to exceed the 10.65 million units produced in 1996/97.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities such as investments in stocks.

Toyoda Automatic Loom Works Ltd, which produces car components and assembles Toyota's Starlet compact car and Sprinter Carib compact station wagon, said it boosted its parent current profit by 47.1 percent to 30.64 billion yen ($257 million) in 1996/97.
It forecast a 32 billion yen ($268 million) parent profit for the current year, up 4.4 percent.

"A weak yen, cost-cutting and relatively good domestic sales of the new Starlet and Sprinter Carib, and of industrial machinery, helped us to post better profits last year. This year, we plan to boost output of the Carib by 30 percent from 39,000 units last year, as we started exporting the new Sprinter Carib to Europe in April," a Toyoda Automatic spokesman said. The firm is owned 23 percent by Toyota.

Aisin Seiki Co Ltd, a component maker, boosted parent current profit by 22.3 percent from a year earlier to 18.75 billion yen ($157 million) in 1996/97, mainly helped by cost-cutting, a spokesman said. Aisin is owned 22.6 percent by Toyota.
"We expect a decline in earnings this year mainly because of an increase in personnel costs resulting from a wage increase for 1997/98," an Aisin spokesman said.
A fire in early February at an Aisin Seiki plant halted supplies of brake parts to Toyota, causing the idling of all Toyota plants for a few days in February.

Aisin had an extraordinary loss of 7.8 billion yen ($65.5 million) in 1996/97 due to the fire. It plans to spend eight billion yen ($67.2 million) this year on a new factory and facilities for brake parts.

Its total investment in 1997/98 will be 38 billion yen ($319 million) up from 29.30 billion a year earlier, he said. Its depreciation costs will rise by 1.7 billion yen ($14.2 million) this year from 24.5 billion yen ($206 million) a year earlier.

Toyota Tsusho Corp, Toyota's trading arm, raised its current profit by 35.6 percent to 9.57 billion yen ($80.4 million) in 1996/97. It forecast parent current profit of 10 billion yen ($84.0 million) for 1997/98 on expectations of higher exports of Toyota cars.

Toyoda Machine Works Ltd boosted its earnings by a steep 120.3 percent to 6.68 billion yen ($56.1 million) in 1996/97, helped by higher domestic sales and exports of machine tools and car parts. Toyota Machine is 22.7 percent owned by Toyota. Its sales to Toyota accounted for 73 percent of its overall sales.

It forecast current profit of eight billion yen ($67.2 million) for 1997/98, up 19.7 percent, mainly due to higher sales of machine tools and car parts and partly because of the weak yen, a spokesman said.

Toyota Auto Body Co Ltd's earnings in 1996/97 rose 13.7 percent to 6.78 billion yen ($56.9 million) mainly because of rationalisation and sales of assembled recreational vehicles to Toyota, a company spokesman said.

Toyota Auto Body, owned 45.2 percent by Toyota, assembles Toyota's mainstay minivan series: the Estima, Regius, Granvia and Ipsum. It forecast a 10.6 percent gain in its 1997/98 earnings to 7.50 billion yen ($63.0 million). ($1=119 yen)
